calibration: winner_in_my_two: NO — my two were Gethin and Constitution Hill; the winner was my SECOND danger, and the sheet's own line for him was 'if he dictates a slow one and Gethin fights for his head, Pride Of Arras beats him' — which is what happened
column8: ERROR (one sentence): I wrote the winner's exact winning scenario as 'what would make me wrong' and picked against it for the third time today — I took the horse with three runs on the surface to write about (Gethin, exposed, 116 here) over the horse with the higher ceiling on my own Blanco line (Pride Of Arras, a G2 winner who ran 117 setting the pace two starts back), the volume-over-weight fault in its third coat; and I named Constitution Hill the danger on the NAME when the numbers I had written (113 in a novice, 164 days, a jumps yard) said he was the fourth-best horse, which he was
column9: CALIBRATION: (1) THE PACE LINE WAS RIGHT AND THE PICK IGNORED IT: 'the leader is likely Pride Of Arras with Gethin on his quarters; Gethin PULLS' — on Polytrack at 1m4f in a 5-runner race the dictating G2 winner is the best horse; the sheet had it; the verdict did not use it. (2) ODDS-ON IN A GROUP 3 ON THE ALL-WEATHER: the rulebook's #14 AW caution and the odds-on bar both said no bet; I stated them and picked anyway 'to test whether I can name the winner' — I could not, and the record now holds the receipt: the cautions are the method, not decoration. (3) THE DANGER-BY-NAME: Constitution Hill got the danger slot because of who he is on a Tuesday at Cheltenham, not what the figures said he is on a Saturday at Kempton; the Ascot 2:10 lesson (Heyzoom, the danger by sire) repeated in the same hour. (4) THE THIRD 'WHAT WOULD MAKE ME WRONG' TO COME TRUE TODAY (Haydock: the ground/the champion's engine — First Law; Ascot: the 7lb rise — bit; Kempton: the pace — Pride Of Arras): from the next sitting that line is written BEFORE the verdict and if it names a horse, that horse's decisive line is weighed against the pick's decisive line on the page, in two sentences, and the stronger one is the pick — no more picking against my own scenario. (5) Sittings today: 0 from 3 settled (Rocket Boy 2nd, Archers Bay 3rd, Gethin 2nd), two dangers/second-dangers won, one passed Blanco horse won — the reads are finding the winner and the verdict is not. (6) THE MASTER'S LESSON (his paste: 'a very important lesson to be learned on this one' — the result and ten years of Past Winners): the winners of this race ran to RPR 112-126 — Enable twice, Mostahdaf, Bay Bridge, Kalpana, Giavellotto: GROUP-ONE and GROUP-TWO horses win a Group 3 like this; the DNA is CLASS. Pride Of Arras was the highest-CLASS horse in the field — a Great Voltigeur (G2) winner who ran 117 in a G2 two starts back — and Gethin's ceiling was a Listed win and a G3 second: at level weights the G2 winner beats the Listed winner, and I let three runs on the surface ('course, distance, Polytrack') and the volume of Gethin's local evidence outweigh the class ladder — 'best horse wins' means the best horse by CLASS, not by the number of lines that fit today's conditions. Second half of the lesson: the pace read was WRONG (Gethin LED and hung left; Pride Of Arras came from off him) and the class horse won ANYWAY — pace is colour, class is the fact. Third: Beckett had won this race before (2017, Chemical Charge) — the yard's record in the race was on the Past Winners page and I did not have it. Proposed wording for his validation: 'In a Group race the best horse is the horse with the highest class achievement at level weights; surface, course and distance lines never outrank a class the horse has already shown.' (7) THE MASTER: 'so why did you miss the obvious — the bookies tricked you'. The obvious: a Group 3 whose ten winners ran 112-126 had a horse whose best is ~116 priced at 8/11 — as if he were Enable — while the only Group 2 winner in the field, the class horse, sat at 11/2-13/2 and DRIFTED; and the second favourite at 7/2 was a famous name with two novice wins. The 8/11 was the bait: it made the exposed local-form horse LOOK like the best horse, the name soaked up the rest of the market, and the class horse was left at a price. I asked the bookmaker's question and then answered it with the bookmaker's answer — 'why odds-on? because he is the best horse on every figure... fair, nothing to argue' — the question exists to make me SUSPICIOUS of a short price, not to ratify it; the odds-on bar and the AW caution are the master's fences against exactly this and I stepped over both. THE SCAR: when the favourite is odds-on and the race's DNA says a higher class wins it, the odds-on price is the trick, not the evidence — the class horse at a price is the pick or the race is a pass.
